title: Salt Creek Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Salt Creek wells have a 32-foot median depth, but costs vary with completion, pump, trenching, and electrical work.
h1: Salt Creek, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Salt Creek is a plains-area community in Pueblo County, about one mile from Blende and two miles from Pueblo. DWR records show 3,562 permitted wells within five miles, with 2,476 recorded as constructed. The local profile is unusually shallow overall: the median reported depth is 32 feet, and the middle half runs from 25 to 40 feet.

That does not make every lot predictable. The records include wells as deep as 1,795 feet, and only 164 wells report a pump yield. Use these figures to set expectations and compare a property with nearby permits, not as a guarantee for a particular parcel.

sections.heading: Salt Creek wells are usually shallow, with exceptions
sections.html:
For Salt Creek and the surrounding five-mile area, the median well depth is 32 feet. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 25 and 40 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 50 feet. A full 97% are under 100 feet. That is the depth range a driller is most likely to discuss for ordinary local conditions.

The record also contains a small deep-well tail: 1% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 1% from 300 to 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,795 feet. Salt Creek sits on alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, while permits commonly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Local geology and the exact lot still control the bid.

sections.heading: Reported yields are generally usable, but verify the lot
sections.html:
The 164 wells with reported pump yields show a median of 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 11.8 to 36.2 gallons per minute. Sixty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 34% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Low production is uncommon in this record but not absent: 5% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% report less than 1 gallon per minute. These figures describe reported pump tests, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the neighboring permits, construction reports, and any available production test. A domestic well also needs the correct DWR permit and must follow its allowed uses and pumping limits.

sections.heading: Water levels are close to the surface and not dropping in this record
sections.html:
Only 120 wells report a static water level, so this is a smaller dataset than the depth record. Among those measurements, the median depth to water is 19 feet, with the middle half between 12 and 25 feet below the surface. That shallow water level can simplify drilling, but it also means construction and sealing details matter.

The decade figures do not show a clear long-term decline. Median depth to water was 20 feet in the 1960s, 20 feet in the 2010s, and 17 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements come from different wells and locations, so they are a local indication rather than a parcel-specific forecast. Confirm the current water level and seasonal conditions with a driller.

sections.heading: Permit history points to steady local drilling activity
sections.html:
Salt Creek’s permit history extends through a newest permit year of 2025. Permits issued by decade were 111 in the 1950s, 178 in the 1960s, 318 in the 1970s, 123 in the 1980s, 382 in the 1990s, 431 in the 2000s, 493 in the 2010s, and 206 in the 2020s.

The largest named share of drilling records belongs to Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 625 records. Don Stewart & Son Drilling, listed as Stewart, Donald D, appears on 250, and Hoffman, listed as Hoffman, Earl, appears on 41. These names describe permit records, not a recommendation or proof that a driller is available today. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the proposed construction method before signing.

sections.heading: A median-depth Salt Creek well is only part of the project cost
sections.html:
For alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 32 feet, the drilled hole models to about $1,100 to $1,800. That is not the finished-water-system price.

Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled finished-well total is about $7,100 to $13,800. A bid can move outside that range if the lot needs greater depth, difficult access, extra casing or grout, unusual electrical work, or longer utility trenches. Get the written scope broken into drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, testing, trenching, and electrical items so competing bids cover the same work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Environmental screening within about 10 miles identifies 49 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 32 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 2 historic mine features. That map does not prove a problem on a specific parcel, but it is enough reason to test a new or existing well and review nearby land uses. Ask for the well’s laboratory results, construction report, and treatment history.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk remains possible even with strong local medians. Before buying or building, locate the proposed well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house together. Confirm setbacks, access for a rig, casing and grout requirements, and the permitted household use. Where water rights are constrained, an augmentation plan may be required. Have a Colorado water professional review the permit before closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Salt Creek, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Salt Creek is 32 feet. The middle half ranges from 25 to 40 feet, and 97% of wells are under 100 feet. The record is not uniform: some wells are much deeper, including a deepest reported depth of 1,795 feet. A nearby permit is useful evidence, but it cannot guarantee the depth on a new lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Salt Creek?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 32-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $1,100 to $1,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work models to about $7,100 to $13,800. Ask for a written scope because depth, access, casing, equipment, and trench length can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Salt Creek wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 164 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 11.8 to 36.2 gallons per minute. Sixty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Treat these as area records, not a guarantee; request a local production test when possible.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Salt Creek?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, the mapped record includes 49 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 32 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 2 historic mine features. Have the well tested by a qualified laboratory, review prior results, and identify treatment needs before relying on the water for a home.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Salt Creek?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a clear decline. Depth to water was 20 feet in the 1960s, 20 feet in the 2010s, and 17 feet in the 2020s. Only 120 wells report static water levels, and they are not all at one location. Check the current static level and nearby well history for the specific parcel.
